notes.definition: Algae and plants decreased the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere by photosynthesis. Carbon dioxide was also decreased by the formation of sedimentary rocks (such as limestone) and fossil fuels (coal, crude oil and natural gas) that contain carbon.
explanation: The Earth's early atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide. Today carbon dioxide makes up only about 0.04% of the atmosphere. Several processes removed it. Some carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans when they formed, and carbonates were precipitated as sediments. Then, once algae and plants had evolved, photosynthesis removed large amounts: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂). The carbon became part of the organisms.

Carbon dioxide was also removed by the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels that contain carbon. These processes locked carbon away in the Earth's crust for millions of years instead of letting it return to the atmosphere.

Limestone is a sedimentary rock made mainly of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃). Many marine organisms used dissolved carbon dioxide to build shells and skeletons of calcium carbonate. When they died, their remains settled on the sea bed and were buried by more sediment. Over millions of years they were compressed to form limestone.

Coal is a sedimentary rock formed from thick plant deposits. Plants that grew in swamps died and were buried before they could fully decay. Over millions of years, heat and pressure turned the buried plant material into coal. Crude oil and natural gas formed from deposits of plankton (tiny sea organisms) that were buried in mud on the sea bed. Heat and pressure over millions of years, with little oxygen, changed them into crude oil and natural gas, which are trapped in porous rocks.

You need to be able to describe the main changes in the atmosphere over time and their likely causes. Carbon dioxide decreased (dissolving in oceans, photosynthesis, sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels), oxygen increased (photosynthesis), and nitrogen gradually built up (released by volcanoes and very unreactive). When fossil fuels are burned today, the carbon locked up in them is released again as carbon dioxide.
keyFacts: The early atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide; today it is about 0.04%.
Algae and plants decreased carbon dioxide by photosynthesis.
Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans, and carbonates were precipitated as sediments.
The formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels containing carbon also decreased carbon dioxide.
Limestone (mainly calcium carbonate, CaCO₃) formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms.
Coal formed from thick deposits of plant material buried in swamps.
Crude oil and natural gas formed from plankton buried in mud on the sea bed.
All these processes took millions of years and involved burial, heat and pressure.

keyTerms.definition: Rock formed from layers of sediment that are compressed over millions of years, for example limestone and coal.
A sedimentary rock made mainly of calcium carbonate, formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms.
A fuel formed over millions of years from the remains of living organisms: coal, crude oil and natural gas.
Tiny organisms that live in the sea; their buried remains formed crude oil and natural gas.
CaCO₃, the main compound in limestone and in many shells and skeletons.
The process in which algae and plants use light to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.

workedExamples.title: Percentage decrease in carbon dioxide
workedExamples.question: Example data: suppose an early atmosphere contained 95% carbon dioxide and it is now 0.04%. Calculate the percentage decrease.
workedExamples.answer: 99.96% decrease (almost all the carbon dioxide was removed).

workedExamples.title: Carbon locked up in limestone
workedExamples.question: Calculate the mass of carbon in 250 g of pure calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16.

workedExamples.title: Ordering the changes
workedExamples.question: Put these in the order they happened: oxygen gradually increases; volcanoes release mainly carbon dioxide; oceans form and carbon dioxide dissolves; algae begin photosynthesis.
steps: First the volcanoes form the early atmosphere.
Water vapour condenses into oceans, and carbon dioxide dissolves in them.
About 2.7 billion years ago algae begin photosynthesis.
Oxygen then gradually increases as plants evolve, while carbon dioxide keeps falling.
workedExamples.answer: Volcanoes release CO₂; oceans form and CO₂ dissolves; algae begin photosynthesis; oxygen gradually increases.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think carbon dioxide was removed only by plants.
misconceptions.right: In fact it was also removed by dissolving in the oceans and by forming sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think coal and crude oil formed from the same organisms.
misconceptions.right: In fact coal formed mainly from plant deposits in swamps, while crude oil and natural gas formed from plankton buried in sea-bed mud.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think limestone formed from volcanic lava.
misconceptions.right: In fact limestone is a sedimentary rock formed from the calcium carbonate shells and skeletons of marine organisms.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think fossil fuels form in a few years.
misconceptions.right: In fact they take millions of years of burial, heat and pressure, which is why they are non-renewable.

realWorld: The White Cliffs of Dover are chalk, a type of limestone made from the shells of tiny marine organisms.
Coal seams in the UK, for example in South Wales, formed from swamp forests about 300 million years ago and sometimes contain fossil plant leaves.
Burning fossil fuels today releases carbon that was locked away for millions of years, increasing carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
examTips: When asked how carbon dioxide decreased, give several processes: dissolving in oceans, photosynthesis, formation of sedimentary rocks, formation of fossil fuels.
Match each deposit to its origin: limestone from shells and skeletons, coal from plants, crude oil and natural gas from plankton.
Use the phrases 'buried', 'compressed', 'heat and pressure' and 'millions of years' when describing formation.
In 'describe the main changes' questions, cover all three gases: carbon dioxide down, oxygen up, nitrogen up.
summary: Photosynthesis by algae and plants decreased carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide dissolved in oceans and carbonates formed sediments.
Limestone formed from shells and skeletons of marine organisms.
Coal formed from buried plant deposits.
Crude oil and natural gas formed from plankton buried in mud.
These sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels lock up carbon.
Overall: carbon dioxide down, oxygen up, nitrogen up.

flashcards.front: How did algae and plants decrease carbon dioxide?
flashcards.back: By photosynthesis, which uses carbon dioxide.

flashcards.front: Name two other ways carbon dioxide was removed from the atmosphere.
flashcards.back: Formation of sedimentary rocks and formation of fossil fuels (also dissolving in oceans).

flashcards.front: What is limestone mainly made of?

flashcards.back: Shells and skeletons of marine organisms settled on the sea bed, were buried and compressed over millions of years.
Thick deposits of plant material, buried in swamps.

flashcards.front: What did crude oil and natural gas form from?
flashcards.back: Plankton buried in mud on the sea bed.

flashcards.front: What conditions turn buried remains into fossil fuels?
flashcards.back: Heat and pressure over millions of years, with little oxygen.

flashcards.front: What percentage of the atmosphere is carbon dioxide today?
Why are fossil fuels described as storing carbon?
flashcards.back: The carbon from organisms (originally from atmospheric CO₂) is locked up in them.

flashcards.front: What happens to the stored carbon when fossil fuels are burned?
flashcards.back: It is released as carbon dioxide.

flashcards.front: Name the three main changes to the atmosphere over time.
flashcards.back: Carbon dioxide decreased, oxygen increased, nitrogen increased.
Volcanoes released it and it is very unreactive, so it was not removed.

questions.question: Which process carried out by algae and plants decreased carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
markScheme: 1 mark: photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide. Respiration, combustion and decay release it.

questions.question: What is limestone mainly made of?
markScheme: 1 mark: calcium carbonate
questions.explanation: Limestone is mainly calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, from shells and skeletons of marine organisms.

questions.question: Which fossil fuel formed mainly from plant deposits?
markScheme: 1 mark: coal
questions.explanation: Coal formed from thick plant deposits. Crude oil and natural gas formed from plankton.

questions.question: Crude oil and natural gas formed from which organisms?
markScheme: 1 mark: plankton buried in mud
questions.explanation: Crude oil and natural gas formed from plankton that were buried in mud on the sea bed.

questions.question: Which type of rock locks up carbon and helped to decrease carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
markScheme: 1 mark: sedimentary rock
questions.explanation: Sedimentary rocks such as limestone contain carbon. Granite is igneous and does not form from carbon dioxide.

questions.question: How did limestone form?
options: From shells and skeletons of marine organisms compressed over millions of years
markScheme: 1 mark: from shells and skeletons of marine organisms compressed over millions of years
questions.explanation: Marine organisms made calcium carbonate shells and skeletons; their remains settled, were buried and compressed.

questions.question: Which change to the atmosphere was not caused mainly by photosynthesis?
markScheme: 1 mark: increase in nitrogen
questions.explanation: Nitrogen built up because volcanoes released it and it is unreactive. Photosynthesis removes CO₂ and releases O₂.

questions.question: Why did plant remains that formed coal not fully decay?
options: They were buried before they could decay.
markScheme: 1 mark: they were buried before they could decay
questions.explanation: Burial in swamps cut off oxygen and stopped decay, so the carbon was kept and later turned to coal under heat and pressure.

Heat and pressure over millions of years

questions.explanation: Fossil fuels form slowly, over millions of years, under heat and pressure in the Earth's crust.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why burning fossil fuels increases carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
options: Fossil fuels contain carbon dioxide gas trapped as bubbles.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon that was removed from the atmosphere millions of years ago and locked up.
Burning fossil fuels makes plants stop photosynthesising.
Fossil fuels contain nitrogen which turns into carbon dioxide.
markScheme: 1 mark: releases locked-up carbon
questions.explanation: The carbon in fossil fuels originally came from atmospheric carbon dioxide via organisms. Combustion turns it back into carbon dioxide.

rows: Looked at the rock with a hand lens

options: It is coal formed from plants.
It is an igneous rock from a volcano.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the results from a model of the early atmosphere.
Calculate the percentage of the carbon dioxide that was removed by photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Fraction removed = 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75 = 75%.

questions.question:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.
Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16
questions.explanation: Add the relative atomic masses: one Ca (40), one C (12) and three O (3 × 16 = 48). 40 + 12 + 48 = 100.

questions.question:
Calculate the mass of carbon in 500 g of pure calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.
Relative atomic mass (Ar): C = 12
Relative formula mass (Mr): CaCO₃ = 100
markScheme: 1 mark: fraction of carbon = 12 ÷ 100
questions.explanation: Carbon is 12% of the mass of CaCO₃. 0.12 × 500 = 60 g.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows estimates of the percentage of carbon dioxide in the Earth's early atmosphere and in the atmosphere today.
Calculate the percentage decrease in the percentage of carbon dioxide.
Give your answer to 4 significant figures.
questions.explanation: 94.96 ÷ 95 = 0.99958, × 100 = 99.96% to 4 significant figures.

questions.question:
Marine organisms make shells of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.
Each mole of CaCO₃ contains the carbon from one mole of CO₂.
Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide removed from the sea water to make 25 g of CaCO₃.
Relative formula masses (Mr): CaCO₃ = 100   CO₂ = 44
markScheme: 1 mark: moles CaCO₃ = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 mol
1 mark: moles CO₂ = 0.25 mol
1 mark: mass CO₂ = 0.25 × 44 = 11 g
questions.explanation: One mole of CO₂ per mole of CaCO₃, so 0.25 mol × 44 g/mol = 11 g.

questions.question: Name two fossil fuels that formed from plankton.
markScheme: 1 mark: crude oil
1 mark: natural gas
questions.explanation: Plankton buried in mud formed crude oil and natural gas. Coal formed from plants.

questions.question: Give the formula of calcium carbonate.
markScheme: 1 mark: CaCO₃
questions.explanation: Calcium carbonate contains Ca²⁺ and CO₃²⁻ ions in a 1 : 1 ratio.

questions.question: Describe how coal was formed.

questions.question: Describe how limestone was formed.

questions.question: Explain how the formation of fossil fuels reduced the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
markScheme: 1 mark: the organisms contained carbon taken from atmospheric carbon dioxide (by photosynthesis or feeding)
1 mark: burial locked the carbon away so it was not returned to the atmosphere by decay or respiration
questions.explanation: Normally decay returns carbon to the air. Burial prevented this, so the carbon stayed out of the atmosphere.

questions.question: Suggest why scientists think limestone deposits are evidence that the early atmosphere contained more carbon dioxide than today.
markScheme: 1 mark: limestone contains large amounts of carbon in carbonate
1 mark: this carbon came from carbon dioxide (dissolved from the atmosphere), so a lot of carbon dioxide must have been removed
questions.explanation: The huge amount of carbon stored in limestone had to come from somewhere: atmospheric carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Explain why water vapour in the early atmosphere led to a decrease in carbon dioxide.
markScheme: 1 mark: water vapour condensed to form oceans
1 mark: carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans (and carbonates were precipitated as sediments)
questions.explanation: The oceans acted as a store for carbon dioxide; carbonates then formed sediments.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows how the Earth's atmosphere has changed.
Describe the main changes in the composition of the atmosphere from the early atmosphere to today.
Give one cause of each change.
markScheme: Indicative content: early atmosphere mainly carbon dioxide, little or no oxygen; carbon dioxide decreased (photosynthesis, dissolving in oceans, sedimentary rocks, fossil fuels) to about 0.04%; oxygen increased (photosynthesis by algae and plants) to about 20%; nitrogen increased (released by volcanoes, unreactive so built up) to about 80%.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): changes to carbon dioxide, oxygen and nitrogen described with a correct cause for at least two.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two changes described with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Cover all three main gases and link each change to a cause.

questions.question: Explain how the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere decreased from the early atmosphere to today. Include the formation of limestone, coal, crude oil and natural gas.
markScheme: Indicative content: early atmosphere mainly carbon dioxide; oceans formed and carbon dioxide dissolved; carbonates precipitated as sediments; algae and then plants photosynthesised: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂; carbon became part of organisms; marine organisms built calcium carbonate shells and skeletons, which settled, were buried and compressed to form limestone; plant deposits in swamps buried and compressed by heat and pressure to form coal; plankton buried in mud and changed by heat and pressure over millions of years to form crude oil and natural gas; carbon locked away in sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels, not returned to the atmosphere.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed, well-organised explanation including photosynthesis and the formation of all four deposits, linked to the removal of carbon dioxide.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): photosynthesis and the formation of at least two deposits described, with some link to carbon dioxide removal.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'plants took in carbon dioxide'.
questions.explanation: The best answers link each process back to carbon being removed from the atmosphere and stored.
